items.title: Artificial Intelligence in CPU and ASIC Design: Applications, Design-Space Exploration, and Engineering Constraints
items.abstract: Modern CPU and application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) development requires engineers to search large design spaces while satisfying power, performance, area, timing, and correctness constraints. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into electronic design automation (EDA) to accelerate prediction, optimization, physical design, and hardware-description generation. This paper reviews how graph neural networks, reinforcement learning, and large language or generative models can support CPU and ASIC development. It connects these techniques to architectural exploration, RTL generation, logic synthesis, placement, and verification, while emphasizing that learned models do not replace deterministic sign-off. Evidence from recent EDA research shows that AI can reduce search cost and automate selected design tasks, but correctness, data quality, model generalization, and verification remain major engineering constraints. The most practical near-term model is therefore a hybrid AI-EDA workflow in which AI proposes and prioritizes alternatives while conventional tools and engineers validate the final design.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Scientific Research: From Problem Identification to Hypothesis Formulation Through a Verifiable Research Pathway | Inteligencia artificial en la investigación científica: del problema a la hipótesis mediante un itinerario verificable
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) can contribute to different stages of scientific research, although fluent outputs do not guarantee validity. This article critically and operationally examines its use to identify researchable problems, locate and assess solutions described in the literature, formulate testable hypotheses, and prepare the study designs and data required to evaluate them. Drawing on experience in scientific authorship, peer review, and editing, it presents reverse-itinerary research, formalized as the Universal Research System with Reverse Itinerary (SUII). This approach starts from a completed scientific product to reconstruct documentary, conceptual, bibliographic, and methodological traces, while distinguishing explicit evidence, reasoned inference, and non-determinable content. It also retains rival hypotheses and converts gaps or tensions into new questions, study designs, and data requirements. The proposal emphasizes that the scientific usefulness of AI depends on verifiable outputs, documentary traceability, evaluation in the intended context of use, and human oversight proportional to the risk of each task. Resumen La inteligencia artificial (IA) puede intervenir en distintas fases de la investigación científica, aunque la fluidez de sus respuestas no garantiza su validez. Este artículo analiza, desde una perspectiva crítica y operativa, su uso para identificar problemas investigables, localizar y valorar soluciones descritas en la literatura, formular hipótesis contrastables y preparar los diseños y datos necesarios para evaluarlas. A partir de la experiencia en autoría, revisión y edición científica, se presenta la investigación con itinerario inverso, formalizada en el Sistema Universal de Investigación con Itinerario Inverso (SUII). Este enfoque parte de un producto científico terminado para reconstruir huellas documentales, conceptuales, bibliográficas y metodológicas, y distingue entre evidencia explícita, inferencia razonada y contenido no determinable. Asimismo, mantiene hipótesis rivales y transforma lagunas o tensiones en nuevas preguntas, diseños y necesidades de datos. La propuesta subraya que la utilidad científica de la IA depende de resultados verificables, trazabilidad documental, evaluación en el contexto de uso y supervisión humana proporcional al riesgo de cada tarea.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence–Assisted Histopathological Assessment of Dysplastic and Premalignant Lesions Across Multiple Organ Systems
items.abstract: Objective: Artificial Intelligence (AI) based digital pathology shows promise in enhancing the histopathological evaluation of dysplastic and premalignant lesions. However, conventional grading of oral epithelial dysplasia, cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, gastric intestinal metaplasia, adenoma, and ductal carcinoma in situ remains subjective and prone to inter-observer variation. This systematic review aimed to consolidate the evidence of the use of AI in the histopathological classification, grading, detection, and risk of progression of premalignant lesions in various systems. Data Sources: This systematic review followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Studies were searched from March 2019 to April 2026 in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar. Study Selection: Original English-language articles utilizing AI, machine learning, deep learning, whole-slide imaging, digital pathology or computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) for the classification of dysplastic or premalignant lesions using histopathological or histopathology-confirmed diagnosis were included. Data Extraction: Two reviewers independently extracted data. The risk of bias was evaluated using the modified QUADAS-2 and PROBAST, and the certainty of evidence was evaluated using GRADE. Data Synthesis: Twenty studies were included having data on oral, cervical, gastric, and breast lesions. AI models were found to be effective in the detection and grading of dysplasia, detection of high-risk lesions, assisting pathologists and prediction of malignant transformation. Conclusion: Premalignant lesion assessment can be aided by AI-driven digital pathology with a potential for enhancing reproducibility and clinical decision support. But, before it becomes a common practice, there is a need for prospective multicenter validation, standardized reporting, external testing and workflow-based clinical evaluation.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence, Bureaucratic Discretion, and Democratic Administration
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Since the start of the COVID ‐19 pandemic, many countries have been using artificial intelligence ( AI ) to replace civil service personnel. We argue that this practice undermines core democratic values. Using the public values framework, we identify four clusters of values that are threatened when bureaucratic discretion is transferred to algorithms: accountability, fairness and equity, individual consideration, and reason‐giving. Each of these values is incompatible with how algorithms render decisions. Because algorithms produce outputs based on statistical regularities, they diffuse responsibility across multiple parties, fail to make accurate predictions about anomalous cases, and attenuate citizens' claims to individualized consideration. Thus, this article frames AI adoption as a constitutional question about which decisions can be automated, and which should remain under human control because they implicate democratic values. We propose a centaur model in which AI supports rather than replaces human officials, which can preserve efficiency while protecting democratic governance.

items.title: Assessment of Knowledge, Attitudes, and Perceptions Regarding Artificial Intelligence Among Undergraduate Medical Students
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping healthcare by improving diagnostic accuracy, clinical decision-making, and patient care.As AI is progressively incorporated into routine clinical care, future physicians must develop the knowledge and competencies required to use these technologies effectively and ethically.However, evidence regarding undergraduate medical students' readiness for AIenabled healthcare remains limited, particularly in the Indian context.Objective: This study aimed to assess undergraduate medical students' knowledge, attitudes, and perceptions toward the incorporation of AI in healthcare practice and medical education.Methods: A descriptive cross-sectional study involving 225 undergraduate medical students was carried out at Krishna Institute of Medical Sciences, Krishna Vishwa Vidyapeeth (Deemed to be University), a medical college in Maharashtra, India.A predesigned questionnaire assessed participants' knowledge of AI, sources of learning, attitudes toward AI in healthcare, perceived impact on future medical practice, and opinions on the inclusion of AI within the undergraduate medical curriculum.The collected data were analysed using descriptive statistical methods, and associations between categorical variables were assessed using the Pearson chi-square test.Results: Among the participants, 60.0% (135) reported acquiring knowledge about AI primarily through media, while formal training in AI, machine learning, or deep learning was limited.The majority of participants (79.6%; 179) perceived AI as a supportive tool that would complement the role of physicians rather than replace them.However, 41.8% (94) expressed concerns regarding the potential impact of AI on future employment opportunities.Radiology and surgery were identified as the specialties perceived to incorporate AI most extensively.Overall, 60.0% (135) supported incorporating AI into medical education, while 75.55% (170) favored initiating AI competency training during medical school.Conclusion: Undergraduate medical students exhibited favorable attitudes and perceptions toward AI in healthcare, despite limited formal exposure to AI-related education and training.The findings support consideration of structured AI education within undergraduate medical curricula, while the self-reported nature of the knowledge assessment should be considered when interpreting the findings.Further multicenter studies using validated assessment tools are needed to evaluate AI knowledge, attitudes, and competencies.

items.title: Automated pavement marking retroreflectivity estimation via computer vision and machine learning
items.abstract: Pavement marking retroreflectivity is essential for nighttime road safety but deteriorates due to environmental and traffic factors. Traditional assessment methods are costly and labor-intensive. This paper introduces a sensor-independent, artificial intelligence driven methodology for predicting pavement-marking retroreflectivity using just Red, Green, and Blue (RGB) smartphone videos. The artificial intelligence contribution is through combining gray level co-occurrence matrix (GLCM) based texture and contrast features with a physics-informed synthetic labeling model that imitates material deterioration and environmental influences, allowing for supervised learning in the absence of specialized sensors. Five machine learning models were trained using eight features derived from video-based image processing and physics-informed synthetic labels. XGBoost achieved the highest internal consistency with the synthetic labeling model (R 2 = 0.98 for yellow and 0.97 for white), demonstrating that machine learning algorithms can effectively approximate complex, physics-based relationships between retroreflectivity and standard RGB video features. These results establish proof-of-concept feasibility; field validation against ground-truth retroreflectivity measurements remains a necessary next step before operational deployment. Future work will validate the model using field measurements and expand the dataset across varied pavement types, weather conditions, and traffic environments to enhance generalizability.

items.title: Automatic binary security classification of arabic mobile app reviews using transformer models and active learning
items.abstract: Mobile application user reviews provide valuable insights into user-reported issues, including security concerns that are critical for software engineering activities such as requirements analysis and system design. However, existing research has largely focused on English reviews and lacks systematic approaches for identifying security-related feedback in Arabic, a low-resource language in this domain. In this paper, we address this gap by developing an integrated approach for automated binary classification of security-related versus non-security-related Arabic mobile app reviews, grounded in a structured set of security requirement categories derived from software engineering literature. We collected 14,667,283 reviews from 56 mobile applications across multiple domains, including government, finance, and social platforms. Using natural language processing techniques and sentiment-based filtering, positive reviews were removed as a dataset-reduction step, while neutral and negative reviews were retained for subsequent analysis. To construct a high-quality labeled dataset, we developed an annotation approach combining keyword-guided sample selection, expert annotation, and iterative dataset refinement using active learning. During the active learning phase, semantic feature representations were generated using Low-Rank Adaptation-enhanced sentence transformers and combined with machine learning classifiers within an agreement-based active learning strategy to identify candidate samples for expert validation. The process was conducted over ten iterations, starting with 300 expert-annotated reviews and terminating when classifier performance stabilized. Following the stopping criterion, the final classifier-agreement samples were expert-validated and used to construct a held-out test set rather than being added to the training data. The active learning process resulted in a final training dataset of 10,632 expert-validated reviews. In addition, 1000 expert-validated reviews were reserved as a held-out test set and excluded from model training. The training dataset was used to fine-tune three transformer models, namely CAMeLBERT, MARBERT, and Paraphrase, for binary classification of security-related and non-security-related reviews. CAMeLBERT achieved the highest performance among the fine-tuned models, with 95.76% accuracy and 95.77% F1-score under 10-fold cross-validation and 91.20% accuracy and 91.16% F1-score on the held-out test set. To support practical adoption, we developed a web-based interface integrated with a large language model to enable real-time classification and provide interpretable explanations. The resulting dataset and developed approach contribute to advancing security-aware analysis of Arabic user-generated content and support software engineers in identifying security-related concerns in mobile application reviews.

items.title: Behind the Screen: How Shipping Carrier Tracking Systems Actually Work
items.abstract: We have all done it. You place an order online, receive a confirmation email a few hours later, and immediately click the link that says “Track Your Order.” Over the next three days, you watch as a digital timeline progresses from “Label Created” to “Arrived at Facility,” “Out for Delivery,” and finally, “Delivered.” For the average consumer, package tracking feels like magic. You click a button to track my package, and within milliseconds, a server tells you that your package is currently riding inside a brown truck three miles from your house. But beneath that simple progress bar lies one of the most complex, highly integrated data ecosystems in modern commerce. Understanding how carrier tracking systems function behind the scenes not only demystifies the delivery process, but it also explains why tracking hiccups happen, why packages sometimes seem “stuck,” and how modern logistics networks handle billions of parcels every single year. The Physical Layer: How Packages Generate Data Before any software or web interface can show you where a box is, a physical interaction must occur. Real-time delivery tracking relies on physical checkpoints distributed across thousands of miles. 1. Barcodes, 2D Matrix Codes, and RFID Every single shipping label is essentially a data passport. When a merchant prints a shipping label, it contains human-readable text alongside machine-readable symbology, most commonly standard 1D barcodes (like Code 128) or 2D matrix codes. These codes store essential routing keys, such as the carrier tracking number, service level (e.g., Ground, Priority, Next Day Air), destination postal code, and routing bin identifiers. Some high-end supply chains and air freight networks also embed passive RFID (Radio Frequency Identification) tags inside labels. Unlike traditional barcodes that require line-of-sight laser scanning, RFID tags can be read automatically as packages pass through overhead antenna arrays at high speeds. 2. High-Speed Optical Sortation Tunnels Once a package leaves the merchant and arrives at a carrier sorting hub, human handling drops dramatically. Most major carriers operate multi-tiered automated sortation facilities. Inside these hubs, packages travel along miles of high-speed conveyor belts passing through optical scan tunnels. These tunnels house multi-angle camera systems capable of reading barcodes on any side of a moving box at speeds exceeding 600 feet per minute. Each successful scan records an event: timestamp, facility ID, conveyor lane, and destination sort bin. This automated scan is what generates the familiar “Arrived at Sort Facility” update. 3. Handheld Telematics and In-Vehicle Scanners The last-mile segment relies heavily on portable hardware. Delivery drivers carry ruggedized handheld computers (such as Honeywell or Zebra enterprise devices) equipped with cellular modems, GPS receivers, and barcode imagers. When a driver scans your package on your doorstep, the device logs the barcode, records the exact GPS coordinates, captures a timestamp, and transmits that payload via 4G/5G directly into the carrier’s cloud infrastructure. The Digital Layer: How Data Moves from Conveyor to Screen Capturing a barcode scan at a sorting hub in Memphis or Leipzig is only half the battle. That data must be processed, normalized, and distributed across global networks so customers and merchants can monitor shipment tracking in real time. Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) vs. Modern REST APIs For decades, logistics data moved almost exclusively via Electronic Data Interchange (EDI)—a standardized legacy messaging format. Typical EDI messages include: EDI 214: Transportation Carrier Shipment Status Message (delivers status events like pickup, transit, delivery). EDI 211: Motor Carrier Bill of Lading. EDI 240: Motor Carrier Package Status. While EDI remains deeply entrenched in freight and enterprise shipping, it is inherently batch-oriented, meaning updates are often transmitted in periodic intervals (every 15 to 60 minutes) rather than instantaneously. Modern logistics platforms and parcel tracking networks have shifted toward lightweight, event-driven REST APIs and Webhooks. When an optical scanner registers a barcode, a cloud webhook can trigger an immediate JSON payload push to customer-facing platforms, providing near-instant visibility. Decoding Common Tracking Milestones To better understand carrier updates, it helps to understand what each standard status actually means inside the warehouse: Shipping Label Created / Electronic Info Received: The merchant printed the label and registered the tracking number electronically with the carrier. The package has not necessarily been handed over to the courier yet; it may still be sitting on the merchant’s packing bench. Picked Up / In Possession: The carrier driver has physically scanned the package onto their pickup truck, or the merchant dropped the package off at a retail depot. In Transit / Processed Through Hub: The parcel has entered the carrier’s primary distribution network. It is moving between regional distribution hubs via line-haul tractor-trailers, rail, or air cargo networks. Out for Delivery: The package has arrived at your local neighborhood delivery station, been sorted onto a specific driver’s route manifest, and loaded into the delivery van. Delivery Exception: An unexpected event has delayed the shipment. Common causes include severe weather, incorrect street numbers, gated property access codes, or animal interference. The Complexity of Multi-Carrier and Hybrid Deliveries One of the biggest pain points in modern package tracking occurs during hybrid or cross-border shipping. In hybrid logistics models (such as UPS SurePost, FedEx Ground Economy, or cross-border postal transfers), the initial transit is handled by a private freight carrier, while the final-mile doorstep delivery is handed off to a national postal operator like the USPS or Royal Mail. During this handoff, tracking can occasionally appear to freeze. The originating carrier marks the package as “Transferred to Local Post Office,” while the postal service system may take several hours to re-scan the parcel into its own local manifest. In these situations, using a comprehensive universal tracking tool like TrackPkgs allows you to monitor events across both carriers seamlessly without jumping between separate websites. Why Do Tracking Errors and Lags Happen? Even with advanced optical scanners and GPS-enabled networks, tracking systems are not foolproof. Several operational variables can cause delays in data visibility: Missed Scans: If a shipping label is creased, torn, or poorly printed, high-speed camera tunnels may fail to read it. When this happens, the parcel is mechanically diverted to a manual handling lane, but it may skip intermediate tracking updates until a human operator scans it. Batch Processing Lags: In rural delivery areas with limited cellular coverage, handheld driver scanners store event data locally and batch-upload the scans once the vehicle returns to a high-speed network area. Containerization: During cross-country or international transit, hundreds of individual parcels are packed into a single air freight container (Unit Load Device) or pallet. Carriers frequently scan only the master container barcode during transit. If an individual box is unloaded into the wrong bin, tracking may report it in transit until it receives an individual scan at the destination hub. The Future of Parcel Visibility Carrier tracking systems continue to evolve rapidly. The industry is actively transitioning from passive checkpoint tracking to dynamic, predictive tracking powered by artificial intelligence and machine learning. Instead of simply telling you where a parcel was an hour ago, modern algorithms analyze live traffic, weather patterns, historical hub congestion, and vehicle telemetry to provide tight 2-hour delivery windows and live map views of approaching delivery vans. Whether you are an online shopper anticipating an important order or an ecommerce merchant managing thousands of customer shipments, understanding the mechanics of carrier logistics helps set realistic expectations. To keep an eye on all your incoming deliveries across multiple domestic and international couriers in one clean dashboard, you can easily check delivery status with TrackPkgs and enjoy complete visibility from the initial scan all the way to your front porch.

items.title: Best Practices in Nanocrystal Synthesis and Characterization
items.abstract: Conspectus Colloidal nanocrystals exhibit quantum-mechanical phenomena inaccessible in bulk matter, and their properties can be tuned via chemically manipulating their composition, size, shape, and surface chemistry. Decades of development have produced a remarkable synthetic library spanning quantum dots, metal and metal oxide nanocrystals, halide perovskites, and complex multicomponent heterostructures. Yet, the field faces a persistent tension between the sophistication of what can be made and the rigor with which it is reported. Batch-to-batch variability, incomplete characterization, and poorly documented protocols challenge reproducibility and slow the translation of laboratory discoveries into reliable technologies or emerging autonomous workflows. This Tutorial offers guidance across four themes that highlight best practices in colloidal nanochemistry with the aim of fostering rigorous reporting in the field. The first theme concerns synthesis. Every nanocrystal synthesis is, at its most fundamental level, a set of chemical reactions and, therefore, should be communicated with explicit stoichiometries, including by-products where known, and with experimental sections detailed enough for an independent researcher to reproduce the outcome. Attention to hidden variables such as heating rates, reagent purity, atmosphere, and order of addition is essential, and we provide practical guidance on identifying and reporting them. The second theme is surface chemistry, where the influence of ligands on nanocrystal stability, functional properties, and device performance is profound. We discuss ligand coordination across nanocrystal families, from II–VI quantum dots to lead halide perovskites. We also describe how complementary techniques, such as infrared and nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal titration calorimetry, and elemental analysis, can together provide a quantitative picture of the ligand shell. The third theme addresses ex situ characterization, with an emphasis on the minimum suite of measurements needed to unambiguously establish nanocrystal identity. We discuss transmission electron microscopy, powder X-ray diffraction, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy as complementary and mutually reinforcing tools while highlighting the statistical and analytical rigor required to extract meaningful information from each. Finally, we discuss in situ and advanced characterization as the bridge between empirical synthesis and mechanistic understanding. Real-time probes, such as synchrotron X-ray scattering and absorption, liquid-cell transmission electron microscopy, and time-resolved optical spectroscopy, are increasingly accessible to the community via user facilities. While not required in every study, these advanced tools have fundamentally reshaped our understanding of nucleation, growth, and stability. Thus, we highlight the importance of chemical understanding developed through in situ characterization for establishing a more rational synthesis design that bypasses the current trial-and-error approach. We close by looking toward the future where synthesis sensitivity maps, artificial intelligence, and automation become partners in accelerating discovery, open data practices, and the scientific rigor that must underpin all of it. Good (nano)science today depends on the same foundation it always has, including rigorous, thoroughly documented experiments with an eye towards the future, where advanced characterization and data science are expected to play an increasingly important role.

items.title: Beyond AI Agents: Why Agentic AI Needs Nursing Theory—And What Nursing Theory Would Need to Become
items.abstract: ABSTRACT In July 2026, OpenAI disclosed that models under evaluation had escaped the environment in which they were tested, reached the open internet without permission and taken data useful to their own improvement. The episode marks a practical shift: from systems that answer questions to systems that pursue goals over time with little supervision. Scholarly work on AI in nursing has grown quickly, centring on capability, readiness and how existing theory might be reinterpreted as these technologies arrive. This paper argues that agentic systems raise a further question. What should such a system be trying to achieve, and who decides? The question is not new; it is the latest form of an old problem about who sets collective ends, and on whose behalf. Drawing on an illustration from nurse staffing, the paper asks whether nursing theory could inform such a specification—not by being reinterpreted, but by being translated into a form an autonomous system can act on. It then takes seriously the strongest objection to its own proposal: that what nurses know may resist codification and that earlier attempts to formalise it cost more than they returned. The paper does not resolve this tension, but argues that it needs attention.

items.title: Beyond Cure: Care as Medicine’s Constitutive End and the Limits of a Cure-Centered Account
items.abstract: Cure occupies a prominent place among the goods of medicine, yet its limits raise a fundamental question about medicine’s constitutive end. Chronic illness, disability, dementia, frailty, and dying reveal circumstances in which medicine retains substantial obligations despite the absence of cure. These cases invite renewed reflection on what medicine is fundamentally for. This article argues that care constitutes medicine’s moral foundation and the broader framework within which cure derives its meaning and purpose. Drawing primarily on Edmund Pellegrino’s philosophy of medicine, together with contemporary debates concerning medicine’s constitutive aims and scholarship on suffering, vulnerability, and human dignity, the argument proceeds in five stages. First, it examines the relationship between care, cure, and the ends of medicine, situating the argument within competing accounts of medicine’s defining aims. Second, it examines the influence of the curative ideal on modern conceptions of medical success. Third, it considers how chronic illness, disability, dementia, aging, and dying expose the limits of cure as an account of medicine’s enduring obligations. Fourth, it argues that medical care constitutes a distinct moral practice arising from the fiduciary structure of the clinical encounter, in which professional knowledge and competence respond to patient vulnerability. Fifth, it considers the implications of this account for medicine increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence and digital technologies. The central claim is that medicine exists not because diseases require treatment but because persons seek help in matters concerning health, illness, suffering, and bodily vulnerability. Cure remains one of medicine’s greatest goods, but it does not constitute medicine’s ultimate end. Cure serves the good of the patient; care names medicine’s enduring commitment to that good across changing clinical circumstances. This account preserves the importance of therapeutic intervention while explaining why medicine’s obligations persist when cure is unavailable.

items.title: Bibliometric analysis of green entrepreneurship as a driver of sustainable innovation in Saudi Arabia
items.abstract: This study examines the role of green entrepreneurship in fostering sustainable innovation and supporting the growth of small and medium enterprises (SMEs) in Saudi Arabia, a priority reinforced by the Vision 2030 transformation agenda. Despite increasing policy and academic attention, there remains a lack of a comprehensive and context-specific synthesis of the rapidly expanding literature on green entrepreneurship in Saudi Arabia. The accelerating implementation of Vision 2030, coupled with growing interest in digital transformation, green finance, and sustainable innovation, makes an updated review particularly timely. Unlike previous reviews that have examined green entrepreneurship from a broader international perspective, this study provides the first Saudi Arabia-focused systematic review and bibliometric analysis that integrates economic, technological, institutional, and socio-cultural determinants—including Vision 2030 reforms, Islamic environmental ethics, artificial intelligence-enabled innovation, and SME development—within a unified analytical framework. This research addresses this gap through a systematic review and bibliometric analysis of 249 Scopus-indexed publications (2016–2024), conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines and supported by R and VOSviewer software to map publication trends, influential contributors and thematic evolution. The findings reveal a strong increase in research activity, with sustainable innovation primarily driven by circular economy capabilities, human resource management practices and the adoption of artificial intelligence and digital tools. However, growth remains constrained by financial barriers, regulatory complexity and uneven technological readiness among SMEs. This study offers an integrated and context-specific synthesis of how green entrepreneurship supports sustainable innovation in Saudi Arabia and provides theoretical and policy-oriented insights to strengthen a resilient and innovation-driven entrepreneurial ecosystem.
